elements: active tilted photograph panel occupying the main view, with the selected panel state a) through f) rendered large
panel a) unpartitioned original image: one continuous tilted rectangular photograph plane with no grid lines, no tile gaps, and no attention overlay
panel b) 4×4 regular windows: the same photograph split into 16 equal rectangular tiles separated by thin white gaps
panel c) 4×4 offset windows: the same photograph split by a partition grid shifted half a 4×4-window width and height, producing clipped partial windows at the image edges
panel d) 2×2 regular windows: the same photograph split into 4 equal rectangular tiles separated by wider white gaps
panel e) 2×2 offset windows: the same photograph split by a partition grid shifted half a 2×2-window width and height, producing clipped partial windows at the image edges
panel f) 1×1 window: the entire photograph treated as one single window, shown as one tile with an outer border and no internal partition gaps
dynamic panel letter at the upper-left of the active main panel: a), b), c), d), e), or f)
dynamic caption centered below the active main panel: Original image, 4×4 windows, 4×4 offset windows, 2×2 windows, 2×2 offset windows, or 1×1 window
comparison-strip mode showing miniature panels a) through f) in sequence from left to right
comparison-strip labels a), b), c), d), e), f) placed above or just to the upper-left of each miniature panel
comparison-strip captions below each miniature panel matching the source captions: Original image, 4×4 windows, 4×4 offset windows, 2×2 windows, 2×2 offset windows, 1×1 window
large horizontal ellipsis glyph between the 4×4 pair c) and the 2×2 pair d) in comparison-strip mode, indicating the hierarchical progression through coarser window groupings
thin dark outer border around every photograph panel and every separated tile
white background or white spacer material visible only in the narrow gaps between partitioned tiles
consistent photograph texture shared across all panels so every tile carries the correct crop of the same source image

interactions.label: Panel view
interactions.teaches: The learner compares the uncut photograph with regular, shifted, coarser, and global window partitions as a single hierarchy rather than as unrelated grids

interactions.label: Show shifted-boundary overlay
interactions.teaches: The learner sees why alternating regular and offset windows lets information cross a boundary that would otherwise separate neighboring tokens

demo_steps.title: Start from the original image
demo_steps.narration: Panel a) is the unpartitioned photograph. It establishes that all later panels are different window cuts of the same image, not different images.

demo_steps.title: Partition into 4×4 local windows
demo_steps.narration: Panel b) cuts the photograph into a 4×4 grid. Each separated tile represents a local self-attention window, so attention is restricted within many small regions.

demo_steps.title: Shift the 4×4 partition
demo_steps.narration: Panel c) shifts the 4×4 partition by half a window in both directions. Turning on the overlay shows how tokens that were separated by a regular boundary can fall inside one shifted window.

demo_steps.title: Move to coarser 2×2 windows
demo_steps.narration: Panel d) shows larger 2×2 windows. The same idea now groups broader image regions, reflecting the hierarchical structure of the Swin Transformer.

demo_steps.title: Shift the 2×2 partition
demo_steps.narration: Panel e) repeats the half-window shift at the coarser level. The shifted layout again changes which neighboring regions can exchange information across the previous boundaries.

demo_steps.title: Degenerate global case
demo_steps.narration: Panel f) treats the whole image as one 1×1 window. This is the global-attention limit: there are no internal window boundaries left.

demo_steps.title: Compare the full a–f sequence
demo_steps.narration: The strip view places all six panels together, including the original image and the ellipsis between the 4×4 and 2×2 stages. The side-by-side comparison makes the alternating regular/offset pattern and the hierarchy of window sizes explicit.

plan.geometry_notes: Use an axonometric tilted-panel presentation resembling the source: each photograph is a very thin rectangular slab, not a deep box. For the large active view, panel local dimensions are X × Y × Z = 3.2 × 4.1 × 0.035 world units, where local X is image width, local Y is image height, and local Z is slab thickness. Rotate the panel so its vertical image edges remain mostly vertical on screen while the top and bottom edges recede upward-right, approximately a 25–35 degree yaw-like tilt. The large active panel is centered slightly above the caption, filling about 70% of frame height. In comparison-strip mode, use six miniature panels each about 0.95 × 1.22 × 0.025 world units, arranged left-to-right with centers roughly at X = -3.3, -2.05, -0.8, 0.8, 2.05, 3.3 and Y = 0; insert a large gray ellipsis '…' at X = 0 between c) and d), with a slightly wider gap there. Panel a) must be a single uncut image plane with no internal grid, no tile separation, no token markers, and no overlays. For regular N×N panels, tile rectangles exactly divide the image into equal N by N crops; b) uses N=4 with 16 equal tiles, d) uses N=2 with 4 equal tiles, and f) uses N=1 with one tile. For offset panels, shift the partition boundaries by half a window width and half a window height relative to the regular grid and clip to the photograph rectangle; c) uses half of a 4×4 window, e) uses half of a 2×2 window. Offset panels should visibly contain smaller clipped edge pieces and larger interior shifted windows. Tile separation gaps: active 4×4 gap about 0.045 world units; active 2×2 gap about 0.07 world units; active 1×1 gap 0. Miniature strip gaps should scale proportionally. Gap color is white #ffffff. Tile borders are dark charcoal #111111, thin, about 0.01–0.015 world units in the active view. Labels and captions are black #111111, with labels a)–f) near the upper-left of each panel and captions centered below. Ellipsis is medium gray #777777. Photograph texture should use the original source photo if available. If not available, procedurally recreate a close graffiti-wall image: light gray concrete wall background #b9bab2 with subtle noise and block seams; central mural/cartoon figure occupying the lower-middle of the frame with black hair/outline #111111, pink/skin face and body tones #e7a0bd and #f2b0c5, a bright yellow shirt or central shape #e2c51a, red graffiti strokes #d7192f crossing the upper/right wall, cyan-blue patches #7fc7d9 and #3d9fc7, off-white wall edges #e5e2d7, and scattered black spray-paint contours. The same full texture and UV coordinate system must be used for all panels; each tile samples the crop corresponding to its position in the original image. Optional teaching overlay is hidden by default: when enabled on c) or e), draw the regular-grid ghost as semi-transparent blue-gray lines #4a90e2 at about 25% opacity, place two small token dots #ff7a00 and #1f77ff on either side of a boundary near the center of the image, and draw a subtle curved bridge #7a3cff at about 45% opacity only if the shifted partition groups them together. Do not show attention links, yellow selected-window highlights, colored token markers, or neighbor outlines in the default figure.
plan.notes: Implement panels as UV-mapped plane or very thin box meshes. For partitioned views, create one mesh per visible window piece using UV rectangles into the shared image texture; do not duplicate or rescale the photograph independently per tile. Compute regular partitions from normalized image coordinates [0,1]×[0,1]. Compute offset partitions by translating the partition lattice by half the regular window size in both axes, then clipping resulting rectangles to the image bounds. Keep panel labels and captions as SDF text or high-resolution sprites that face the camera enough to remain readable while preserving the tilted-panel look. The panelView toggle should replace the main scene contents cleanly: single-panel states show one large panel, while Full a–f strip shows all six miniatures plus the ellipsis. The teaching overlay should be opt-in and should never appear in panel a), panel f), or the default Full a–f strip unless the learner explicitly enables it.

authoredPrompt: This figure shows six panels labeled a) through f) illustrating the hierarchical windowed self-attention partitioning scheme used in the Swin Transformer. Panel a) shows the original photograph as the reference. In the remaining panels the partitions are shown as the photograph cut into slightly separated tiles with thin white gaps between them, each panel drawn with a slight 3D tilt: panels b) and c) show the image divided into 4×4 non-overlapping windows and the same 4×4 grid offset (shifted) by half a window width and height; panels d) and e) show 2×2 windows and their offset variant; and panel f) shows the degenerate 1×1 case in which the entire image is treated as a single attention region (panel captions read '4×4 windows', '4×4 offset windows', '2×2 windows', '2×2 offset windows', '1×1 window'). The figure demonstrates the Swin Transformer's shifted-window strategy: by alternating between regular and offset window partitions across successive transformer layers, the model enables information to flow across window boundaries without the quadratic cost of global self-attention.
authoredInteractions:
- Slider for window size (1 → 2 → 4): step through panels f (1×1), d (2×2), and b (4×4), refining the partition grid overlaid on the photograph and increasing the number of attention windows
- Toggle between regular and offset windows: shift the grid by half a window in both x and y (switching between panels b↔c or d↔e) and highlight how tokens that were split across a boundary in the regular grid share a single window in the offset grid
- Click on a window tile: highlight all tokens inside that tile and show the self-attention connections confined to those tokens, contrasting with a neighboring tile to illustrate the locality constraint at that window size

interactions.label: Window grid: 1×1 → 2×2 → 4×4
interactions.teaches: Increasing the grid level refines the photograph into more local attention windows, moving from one global 1×1 region to 2×2 and then 4×4 local regions

interactions.label: Window alignment
interactions.teaches: A half-window shift changes which neighboring tokens share a window, allowing information to cross boundaries that blocked attention in the regular partition
Self-attention is computed only among tokens inside the clicked window; adjacent windows are visually nearby but are not connected unless a later offset partition groups them together

demo_steps.title: 4×4 local windows
demo_steps.narration: The photograph is partitioned into a 4×4 grid of small attention windows, matching panel b). Clicking a tile shows dense attention inside that tile but no connections crossing into its neighbor.

demo_steps.title: Shift the 4×4 windows
demo_steps.narration: Switching to the offset layout shifts the grid by half a window in both directions, matching panel c). Tokens that were split by a boundary in the regular view can now share one shifted window.

demo_steps.title: Coarser 2×2 windows
demo_steps.narration: At the 2×2 setting, each attention window covers a larger part of the image, matching panel d). The number of windows is smaller, so each selected window contains more tokens.

demo_steps.title: One global 1×1 window
demo_steps.narration: At 1×1, the entire photograph is one attention region, matching panel f). Locality disappears because every token belongs to the same window.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Use one active panel rather than showing all six source panels simultaneously. Panel dimensions: photograph rectangle about 3.2 world units wide by 4.1 world units tall, with its vertical edges kept vertical on screen and its horizontal edges slanting upward to the right like the source panels. Treat the image plane as an upright rectangle yawed about the vertical axis by roughly 35 degrees in an axonometric view. The panel should occupy about 70% of the frame height with caption text below. Use the original graffiti-wall photograph as a texture if available; otherwise approximate it with a gray concrete wall (#bfc0b8), black-haired pink cartoon face/body (#e7a0bd), bright yellow shirt (#e2c51a), red graffiti strokes (#d7192f), cyan/blue patches (#7fc7d9), black outlines, and off-white concrete edges. Base token lattice: 8×8 tokens across the photo, with thin dark gray/black lines about 0.015 world units thick. WindowLevel maps as 0→1×1 window grid, 1→2×2 window grid, 2→4×4 window grid. Regular windows divide the full photo into N×N equal rectangles. Offset windows shift the N×N partition by half a window width and height, clipped to the image frame, producing partial edge windows as in panels c) and e); for 1×1 the offset state should look effectively identical to regular. Window tile separation gap about 0.06 world units for 2×2 and 0.04 world units for 4×4, with black tile borders and white background showing through the gaps. Selected window highlight color: translucent yellow #ffd84d at about 35% opacity. Attention lines inside a clicked window: thin red/orange #ff5533 curves or straight segments connecting token-center markers, with no cross-window lines. Neighboring tile contrast: outline adjacent tile in muted blue #4a90e2 at low opacity but do not draw attention connections to it. Panel caption mapping: windowLevel 2 Regular = b) '4×4 windows'; windowLevel 2 Offset = c) '4×4 offset windows'; windowLevel 1 Regular = d) '2×2 windows'; windowLevel 1 Offset = e) '2×2 offset windows'; windowLevel 0 = f) '1×1 window'.
interactionPlan.notes: Implement the cut-apart tiles as instanced plane meshes with per-tile UV rectangles sampling the same photograph texture, rather than physically slicing an image asset. Recompute tile rectangles whenever windowLevel or shiftedWindows changes. Keep a faint unshifted grid visible in offset mode for comparison, but make it clearly secondary. For click selection, raycast against the visible tile meshes, collect all 8×8 token centers whose positions fall inside that window rectangle, and draw only intra-window attention connections. Use text sprites or SDF text for panel letters and captions so they remain legible in the tilted view.

discrepancies: The original-image panel a) is not implemented as a separate state or view; the figure starts at b) and only covers windowed variants.
The generated figure shows only one panel at a time, while the source presents the full a)-f) comparison sequence side by side with ellipses between groups.
The underlying graffiti photograph is a simplified procedural recreation rather than the source image, with noticeably different drawing proportions, colors, and text details.
Extra attention-link overlays, colored token dots, yellow selection highlighting, and neighbor outlines are visible by default, but these elements do not appear in the source figure.
The panel lacks the source's clean repeated composition spacing and transition ellipses, so the overall multipanel layout is not visually faithful.
The offset and window states are conceptually present, but the default caption/control text adds explanatory semantics not shown in the original figure.
evaluation.notes: The generated model captures the main window-partition idea with useful controls, but it omits the original-image panel and adds attention overlays that make it diverge from the clean source comparison figure.
action_items: Add an explicit a) Original image state with no window partition grid.
Remove the default attention links, colored token markers, yellow highlight, and neighbor outline unless they are hidden behind an optional teaching overlay.
Improve the procedural image texture or use a closer recreation of the source photograph so the panels resemble the original more strongly.
Add visual ellipses or a comparison-strip mode showing b)-f) together to better match the source layout.
plan_action_items: Revise the plan to include the complete a)-f) multipanel comparison, including the unpartitioned original image and the ellipsis-separated sequence.

feedback.rationale: The evaluation explicitly calls for revising the plan to include the full a)-f) multipanel comparison with the original-image panel and ellipses, indicating an incomplete overall structure rather than only implementation polish.

discrepancies: The recreated wall image is only a rough cartoon-like approximation of the source photograph, with noticeably different detail, contrast, and graffiti placement.
The panels are much smaller and more narrowly foreshortened than in the source, making the comparison strip less visually dominant and less like the original layout.
The internal fine token grid appears too coarse compared with the dense grid structure in the source panels.
Panel captions and a–f labels are present but smaller and less prominent than the source figure's large textbook labels.
The oblique/slanted panel perspective is weaker and more edge-on than the source, especially for the original and 1×1 panels.
evaluation.notes: The generated figure correctly captures the six-panel window-partition concept with useful controls, but the photo recreation, scale, grid density, and panel perspective reduce visual fidelity.
action_items: Increase the default strip scale so the six panels fill the canvas more like the source figure.
Adjust the camera/panel yaw to make the panels look closer to the source oblique parallelogram orientation rather than overly narrow slabs.
Use a denser fine grid inside the partitioned windows to better match the source.
Make the a–f letters and bottom captions larger and more prominent.

feedback.rationale: The concept and interaction plan are correct, but the critic identifies concrete rendering fixes—panel scale, yaw/perspective, grid density, and label prominence—that should be handled by the generator.

interactions.label: Panel view
interactions.teaches: The learner compares the uncut photograph with regular, shifted, coarser, and global window partitions as a single hierarchy rather than as unrelated grids

interactions.label: Show shifted-boundary overlay
interactions.teaches: The learner sees why alternating regular and offset windows lets information cross a boundary that would otherwise separate neighboring tokens

demo_steps.title: Start from the original image
demo_steps.narration: Panel a) is the unpartitioned photograph. It establishes that all later panels are different window cuts of the same image, not different images.

demo_steps.title: Partition into 4×4 local windows
demo_steps.narration: Panel b) cuts the photograph into a 4×4 grid. Each separated tile represents a local self-attention window, so attention is restricted within many small regions.

demo_steps.title: Shift the 4×4 partition
demo_steps.narration: Panel c) shifts the 4×4 partition by half a window in both directions. Turning on the overlay shows how tokens that were separated by a regular boundary can fall inside one shifted window.

demo_steps.title: Move to coarser 2×2 windows
demo_steps.narration: Panel d) shows larger 2×2 windows. The same idea now groups broader image regions, reflecting the hierarchical structure of the Swin Transformer.

demo_steps.title: Shift the 2×2 partition
demo_steps.narration: Panel e) repeats the half-window shift at the coarser level. The shifted layout again changes which neighboring regions can exchange information across the previous boundaries.

demo_steps.title: Degenerate global case
demo_steps.narration: Panel f) treats the whole image as one 1×1 window. This is the global-attention limit: there are no internal window boundaries left.

demo_steps.title: Compare the full a–f sequence
demo_steps.narration: The strip view places all six panels together, including the original image and the ellipsis between the 4×4 and 2×2 stages. The side-by-side comparison makes the alternating regular/offset pattern and the hierarchy of window sizes explicit.

plan.geometry_notes: Use an axonometric tilted-panel presentation resembling the source: each photograph is a very thin rectangular slab, not a deep box. For the large active view, panel local dimensions are X × Y × Z = 3.2 × 4.1 × 0.035 world units, where local X is image width, local Y is image height, and local Z is slab thickness. Rotate the panel so its vertical image edges remain mostly vertical on screen while the top and bottom edges recede upward-right, approximately a 25–35 degree yaw-like tilt. The large active panel is centered slightly above the caption, filling about 70% of frame height. In comparison-strip mode, use six miniature panels each about 0.95 × 1.22 × 0.025 world units, arranged left-to-right with centers roughly at X = -3.3, -2.05, -0.8, 0.8, 2.05, 3.3 and Y = 0; insert a large gray ellipsis '…' at X = 0 between c) and d), with a slightly wider gap there. Panel a) must be a single uncut image plane with no internal grid, no tile separation, no token markers, and no overlays. For regular N×N panels, tile rectangles exactly divide the image into equal N by N crops; b) uses N=4 with 16 equal tiles, d) uses N=2 with 4 equal tiles, and f) uses N=1 with one tile. For offset panels, shift the partition boundaries by half a window width and half a window height relative to the regular grid and clip to the photograph rectangle; c) uses half of a 4×4 window, e) uses half of a 2×2 window. Offset panels should visibly contain smaller clipped edge pieces and larger interior shifted windows. Tile separation gaps: active 4×4 gap about 0.045 world units; active 2×2 gap about 0.07 world units; active 1×1 gap 0. Miniature strip gaps should scale proportionally. Gap color is white #ffffff. Tile borders are dark charcoal #111111, thin, about 0.01–0.015 world units in the active view. Labels and captions are black #111111, with labels a)–f) near the upper-left of each panel and captions centered below. Ellipsis is medium gray #777777. Photograph texture should use the original source photo if available. If not available, procedurally recreate a close graffiti-wall image: light gray concrete wall background #b9bab2 with subtle noise and block seams; central mural/cartoon figure occupying the lower-middle of the frame with black hair/outline #111111, pink/skin face and body tones #e7a0bd and #f2b0c5, a bright yellow shirt or central shape #e2c51a, red graffiti strokes #d7192f crossing the upper/right wall, cyan-blue patches #7fc7d9 and #3d9fc7, off-white wall edges #e5e2d7, and scattered black spray-paint contours. The same full texture and UV coordinate system must be used for all panels; each tile samples the crop corresponding to its position in the original image. Optional teaching overlay is hidden by default: when enabled on c) or e), draw the regular-grid ghost as semi-transparent blue-gray lines #4a90e2 at about 25% opacity, place two small token dots #ff7a00 and #1f77ff on either side of a boundary near the center of the image, and draw a subtle curved bridge #7a3cff at about 45% opacity only if the shifted partition groups them together. Do not show attention links, yellow selected-window highlights, colored token markers, or neighbor outlines in the default figure.
plan.notes: Implement panels as UV-mapped plane or very thin box meshes. For partitioned views, create one mesh per visible window piece using UV rectangles into the shared image texture; do not duplicate or rescale the photograph independently per tile. Compute regular partitions from normalized image coordinates [0,1]×[0,1]. Compute offset partitions by translating the partition lattice by half the regular window size in both axes, then clipping resulting rectangles to the image bounds. Keep panel labels and captions as SDF text or high-resolution sprites that face the camera enough to remain readable while preserving the tilted-panel look. The panelView toggle should replace the main scene contents cleanly: single-panel states show one large panel, while Full a–f strip shows all six miniatures plus the ellipsis. The teaching overlay should be opt-in and should never appear in panel a), panel f), or the default Full a–f strip unless the learner explicitly enables it.
